title: Backtracking: Generate All Subsets
oneLiner: Recursion with a choice at every step: include this element or don't, then undo and try the other branch.
keyTakeaway: Backtracking is recursion plus "try a choice, recurse, then undo the choice before trying the next one" -- the undo step is what lets the same current-state variable be reused across every branch instead of copying it. Reach for it whenever a problem wants "all possible ways to do X", not just one answer.
explanation: Generating every subset of a set is a classic backtracking problem. At each recursive call, first record the current partial selection as one valid subset (every prefix of choices is itself a valid subset -- including the empty one). Then, for each remaining element (starting from wherever you left off, so you never re-pick an earlier element and never produce the same subset twice), add it to the current selection, recurse, and then REMOVE it again before trying the next element -- that removal is the "backtrack" step. Because the same `current` list is shared and mutated across the whole recursion (added to on the way down, removed from on the way back up), this uses way less memory than building a fresh copy at every call. Watch out for that exact bug: if you forget to remove the element after recursing (the backtrack step), every subsequent subset silently keeps everything from earlier branches.

recognitionSignals: The problem asks for ALL possible ways to do something (all subsets, all permutations, all valid boards/paths) rather than one answer or a count.
You're making a sequence of choices where each choice needs to be tried, then undone, before trying the next.
A brute-force recursive tree naturally represents the problem, and pruning branches early (backtracking out of a bad partial answer) would help.
gotchas: Forgetting to undo the choice (remove what you just added) after the recursive call returns -- every later branch then silently carries leftovers from earlier ones.

Appending a COPY of the current list when you record an answer, not a reference to the shared mutable list -- otherwise every recorded "answer" ends up pointing at the same list, which later mutates out from under all of them.
The starting index for the inner loop must move forward (start from i + 1, not 0) or you'll regenerate permutations of the same subset instead of each subset once.
confusableWith: Recursion (Fundamentals) is the umbrella concept; backtracking is recursion with the specific "choose, recurse, un-choose" shape used for exploring all possibilities, usually with a shared mutable state instead of passing a new copy down each call.

Dynamic programming (a later lesson) also explores a space of choices, but caches overlapping subproblems to avoid redoing work -- backtracking recomputes everything, which is fine because it's visiting every distinct answer anyway, not solving the same subproblem repeatedly.

complexity.note: There are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each into the result costs up to n; the recursion itself is only n deep (the output list is extra, O(n · 2ⁿ)).

referenceSolutions.python:
def subsets(nums):
    result = []
    current = []

    def backtrack(start):
        result.append(current[:])  # a COPY -- current keeps changing
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            current.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1)
            current.pop()  # undo the choice

    backtrack(0)
    return result
